approachQuestion.prompt:
Ribbon inventory. A ribbon is supplied as r records (code,count). Each record represents count consecutive copies of that fixed-size integer code. Return how many positions of the represented ribbon have a specified target code. Records need not alternate codes, and identical codes may occur far apart. There are 0 <= r <= 200,000 records, each count is between 1 and 1,000,000,000, and the represented length N and answer fit signed 64-bit. The array of records is read-only with constant-time indexed access; all arithmetic on these words is constant time. Choose minimum worst-case time, then auxiliary storage. Return one integer, not an expanded ribbon.

Example 1: Input: records=[(4,3),(9,2),(4,5)], target=4. Output: 8.
Example 2: Input: records=[], target=9. Output: 0.

options.text: For every record whose code equals target, add its count to one total.
options.feedback: Each matching record contributes exactly as many positions as its count, without creating any of those positions individually.

options.text: Create the full ribbon by repeating every code count times, then count target positions.
options.feedback: It computes the right answer but can materialize billions of positions from one tiny record. The count field already states that record’s entire contribution.

options.text: Add one for each record whose code equals target, ignoring count.
options.feedback: For records=[(4,3)], target=4, this returns 1 instead of 3. Records represent multiple positions.

options.text: Return the count of the first record matching target, or zero if none matches.
options.feedback: For [(4,3),(9,2),(4,5)], target=4, the answer is 8, not 3. Matching records can be separated.

feedback.reason: Compressed multiplicities can contribute directly to an aggregate without generating their represented elements.
details: Initialize a total to zero, visit each record once, and add count when code equals target. Return the total. Never expand records or loop count times.

A matching record (target,1000000) contributes its count with one addition. Expanding it into a million positions throws away the benefit of the representation. Separate records with the same target must all contribute; records are not guaranteed to have distinct codes.

“For every record whose code equals target, add its count to one total.”: Each matching record contributes exactly as many positions as its count, without creating any of those positions individually.

“Create the full ribbon by repeating every code count times, then count target positions.”: It computes the right answer but can materialize billions of positions from one tiny record. The count field already states that record’s entire contribution.
“Add one for each record whose code equals target, ignoring count.”: For records=[(4,3)], target=4, this returns 1 instead of 3. Records represent multiple positions.
“Return the count of the first record matching target, or zero if none matches.”: For [(4,3),(9,2),(4,5)], target=4, the answer is 8, not 3. Matching records can be separated.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For add-matching-run-lengths, choose worst-case time and auxiliary space in terms of r stored records and represented length N. Include setup for r=0. Record fields and target are fixed-size words; output and input are excluded.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard bound for the complete execution. Count peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage; exclude supplied input and required output.
Word arithmetic, indexing, and copying one fixed-size element take constant time. No hashing or recursion is used.

feedback.reason: Inspect r compressed records without iterating over their represented multiplicities.
details: There are r comparisons and at most r word additions, plus constant setup. Thus the tight bound is O(r+1), independent of multiplicities N. A total, index, and current fields use constant auxiliary storage. No expanded copy, hashing, or recursion is present.
“O(N + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This counts represented positions, but one large count is added in one word operation rather than repeated that many times.
“O(N + 1) time, O(N + 1) auxiliary space”: Those costs describe materializing a ribbon, which the method never does.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Any record may contribute a target run, so all r records must be inspected in the worst case.
